title: An Antarctic deal, slowing emissions cuts and a 'zero-human company'

stories.headline: Australia and China quietly agree to share Antarctic logistics
stories.headlineZh: 澳中悄然达成南极后勤互助协议
stories.summaryZh: 信息公开文件显示澳中签署南极后勤合作安排，而中国正计划在澳南极领地修建冰上跑道。
stories.c1:
Australia has quietly agreed to share logistical support with China in Antarctica, according to Freedom of Information documents released to the ABC. The arrangement came to light in a briefing prepared for the environment department ahead of Senate estimates, which noted that the Australian Antarctic Division had no cooperative deal with China's Polar Research Institute for the 2025–26 season, but that one for 2026–27 was in development. The foreign affairs department has since confirmed it has been enacted, describing the two countries' cooperation as long-standing.

The precise terms have not been disclosed. The ABC understands, however, that it is a so-called "quid pro quo" arrangement, under which each side typically supports the other's flights, ground transport and emergency assistance. Such deals are far from unusual: Australia struck a similar one with China for 2024–25 and has comparable arrangements with other nations, including France.

What lends the agreement added significance is China's growing footprint on the frozen continent. Beijing plans to build a blue-ice runway in the Grove Mountains, which lie within Australian Antarctic Territory. Its environmental evaluation envisages up to eight flights a year and describes the site as an "aircraft carrier-style hub" for East Antarctica, with an opening expected in 2029–30. China already runs five research stations and intends to add a sixth.

Canberra has been notably guarded. The foreign affairs department declined to say whether it supports the runway, stating only that it expects all parties to uphold the Antarctic Treaty, including its bans on militarisation and mining. Meanwhile, requests for documents about Chinese icebreakers visiting Australian ports were rejected on national security grounds, suggesting the issue is regarded as rather more sensitive than officials let on.
stories.b2:
Australia has agreed to share transport and other support with China in Antarctica. The ABC learned about the deal through Freedom of Information documents. A government briefing said that Australia's Antarctic Division and China's Polar Research Institute were preparing an agreement for the 2026–27 season, and the foreign affairs department says it is now in place.

The details have not been made public. However, the ABC understands that the two sides will help each other with flights, ground transport and emergencies. This kind of deal is quite common. Australia had a similar one with China in 2024–25, and it also has deals with countries such as France.

The agreement matters partly because China is expanding in Antarctica. It plans to build a runway on blue ice in the Grove Mountains, an area inside Australian Antarctic Territory. The runway could handle up to eight flights a year and may open in 2029–30. China already has five research stations and wants to build another one.

The Australian government has said very little. It would not say whether it supports the runway. It only said that all countries should follow the Antarctic Treaty, which bans military activity and mining there. The ABC's requests for documents about Chinese icebreakers in Australian ports were also refused for national security reasons.

vocab.en: to become known, especially after being hidden
vocab.example: The problem only came to light after customers began complaining.

vocab.en: being planned or prepared but not yet finished
vocab.example: A sequel to the film is already in development.

vocab.en: having existed for a long time
vocab.example: The two clubs have a long-standing rivalry.

vocab.en: something given in return for something else
vocab.example: Their support was a quid pro quo for our help last year.

vocab.en: to reach an agreement with someone
vocab.example: The union finally struck a deal with management.

vocab.en: to make something seem more important
vocab.example: The timing lends extra significance to the announcement.

vocab.en: the amount of presence or influence something has in an area
vocab.example: The company has expanded its footprint across Asia.

vocab.en: to imagine or plan something as possible in the future
vocab.example: The council envisages a car-free city centre by 2035.

vocab.en: careful not to give away information or feelings
vocab.example: She gave a guarded answer when asked about her plans.

questions.q: Australia had a logistics deal with China's Polar Research Institute for the 2025–26 season.
questions.explain: 原文说 Antarctic Division "had no cooperative deal" with China's Polar Research Institute "for the 2025–26 season"，与题干相反，故为 False。

questions.q: The full terms of the new agreement have been made public.
questions.explain: 原文说 "The precise terms have not been disclosed"，故为 False。

questions.q: France has expressed concern about China's planned runway.
questions.explain: 原文只提到澳大利亚与法国有 "comparable arrangements"，并未提及法国对跑道的态度，故为 Not Given。

questions.q: What does the writer suggest in the final paragraph?
options: The government strongly opposes China's runway.
Officials may see the issue as more sensitive than they admit.
Chinese icebreakers have been banned from Australian ports.
The Antarctic Treaty allows limited mining.
questions.explain: 最后一段说 "suggesting the issue is regarded as rather more sensitive than officials let on"，即官方可能比公开表示的更在意此事。

stories.discuss: Why do you think countries cooperate in Antarctica even when they are rivals elsewhere? Do you think this kind of cooperation will last as more nations expand their presence there?

stories.headline: Emissions fall, but too slowly for Australia's 2035 target
stories.headlineZh: 澳大利亚排放下降，但速度不足以实现2035年目标
stories.summaryZh: 年度气候声明显示排放下降1.3%，但气候变化局警告减排速度需大幅加快。
stories.c1:
Australia's greenhouse gas emissions are falling, but nowhere near quickly enough to meet the country's 2035 target, according to the government's annual climate statement. Emissions dropped by 1.3 per cent in the year to June, a reduction of 6.2 million tonnes. Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen noted that this year's pace was roughly one and a half times the average of the past decade, yet the fall was smaller than those recorded in the two previous reporting periods.

The Climate Change Authority, which advises the government, struck a more sobering note. The government has committed to cutting emissions by 62 to 70 per cent by 2035, and reaching the upper end of that range would require average cuts of about 30 million tonnes a year, almost five times the current rate. The authority's chair, Matt Kean, described the challenge as "formidable". Modelling suggests Australia is almost on track for its legislated 2030 goal of 43 per cent, although at least one prominent economist doubts even that will be met on time.

The electricity sector remains the bright spot. Its emissions fell 3.6 per cent, and renewables supplied a record 45.9 per cent of power in the National Electricity Market. Transport, by contrast, edged up slightly, as diesel use on the roads and domestic flying increased, despite electric vehicles now making up nearly a quarter of new car sales.

According to Mr Kean, the bottleneck is no longer approving projects but actually building them, with financing, construction and grid connections all lagging behind. He argued that deployment would need to roughly triple, and warned that the nation's reliance on coal and iron ore exports is arguably its greatest economic risk.
stories.b2:
Australia's greenhouse gas emissions are going down, but not fast enough to reach the 2035 target. The government's annual climate statement shows emissions fell by 1.3 per cent in the year to June. That is a drop of 6.2 million tonnes. Minister Chris Bowen said the pace was about one and a half times the average of the last ten years.

The Climate Change Authority gave a more serious warning. The government has promised to cut emissions by 62 to 70 per cent by 2035. To reach 70 per cent, Australia would need to cut about 30 million tonnes every year, almost five times faster than now. The authority's chair, Matt Kean, called this a very difficult task. Australia is close to being on track for its 2030 goal of 43 per cent.

Electricity is the success story. Emissions from the sector fell by 3.6 per cent, and renewable energy produced a record 45.9 per cent of power in the main electricity market. However, transport emissions rose a little because people used more diesel and took more domestic flights.

Mr Kean said the main problem now is building approved projects, not approving them. He believes the country must build about three times faster. He also warned that depending on coal and iron ore exports is a major economic risk.

vocab.en: not at all; far from
vocab.example: The stadium was nowhere near full on Sunday.

vocab.en: to say something serious that makes people less optimistic
vocab.example: The report struck a sobering note about youth unemployment.

vocab.en: the highest part of a range
vocab.example: Prices are at the upper end of what most families can afford.

vocab.en: likely to achieve what is planned
vocab.example: We're on track to finish the project by Friday.

vocab.en: a part of a situation that is good when the rest is not
vocab.example: Tourism was the one bright spot in a weak economy.

vocab.en: to increase slightly and gradually
vocab.example: Petrol prices have edged up again this week.

vocab.en: something that slows down a process
vocab.example: Staff shortages are the main bottleneck in the system.

vocab.en: to move or develop more slowly than others
vocab.example: Rural areas still lag behind cities in internet speed.

vocab.en: the state of depending on something
vocab.example: Our reliance on cars makes the city hard to walk around.

questions.q: Emissions fell by more in the year to June than in the two previous reporting periods.
questions.explain: 原文说 "the fall was smaller than those recorded in the two previous reporting periods"，故为 False。

questions.q: Renewables supplied a record share of power in the National Electricity Market.
questions.explain: 原文说 "renewables supplied a record 45.9 per cent of power in the National Electricity Market"，故为 True。

questions.q: The Climate Change Authority recommended a new carbon tax on diesel.
questions.explain: 原文提到柴油使用增加，但没有提到任何碳税建议，故为 Not Given。

questions.q: According to Matt Kean, what is the main obstacle now?
options: Turning approved projects into working capacity
A lack of public support for renewables
questions.explain: 原文说 "the bottleneck is no longer approving projects but actually building them"。

stories.discuss: Why do you think it is harder to cut emissions from transport than from electricity? What would encourage people in your city to change how they travel?

stories.headline: Sydney founder plans 'zero-human company' run by AI agents
stories.headlineZh: 悉尼创业者计划打造由AI代理运营的“零人公司”
stories.summaryZh: 一家悉尼科技公司推出由聊天机器人销售、AI维护的软件业务，法律专家质疑其说法。
stories.c1:
A Sydney tech founder says he is on the verge of launching what he calls Australia's first "zero-human company". Lambros Photios, who heads the software firm Adaca, has set up Ante, a business that relies on chatbots to sell AI-built productivity software. Developers created the product in roughly ten days by using AI to clone a subscription tool the company had been paying for, and Photios hopes it will be maintained entirely by AI agents, without daily human input, by March.

The appeal is largely financial. A business like this would traditionally need four or five full-time staff, but with chatbots answering customers and AI writing code, Photios argues that labour costs could fall to almost nothing, allowing Ante to undercut its rivals. He is careful, though, to keep AI away from payments and data security, conceding that a hallucination involving financial records simply cannot be risked.

Legal experts are sceptical. Under Australian law, every company must have a director who is held liable when things go wrong, so a genuinely human-free company is impossible. University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson argues that a firm meeting its obligations would really be a sole trader relying heavily on automation, and calls the label "a terrible sleight of hand".

The idea lands at a sensitive moment. Australian tech firms have shed thousands of jobs this year, with an industry body attributing many of the cuts to AI, and entry-level developer roles are drying up. Photios acknowledges a backlash is likely, but hopes AI will ultimately create more business owners than it displaces, perhaps by encouraging laid-off developers to start ventures of their own.
stories.b2:
A tech businessman in Sydney says he will soon run Australia's first "zero-human company". Lambros Photios, the founder of the software firm Adaca, has started a business called Ante. It uses chatbots to sell productivity software made by AI. His developers built the product in about ten days, and he wants AI agents to maintain it without daily human help by March.

The main reason is money. A business like this usually needs four or five full-time workers. Photios says that if chatbots talk to customers and AI writes the code, staff costs could almost disappear, so Ante can charge much less than other companies. However, he does not let AI handle payments or data security, because mistakes there would be too dangerous.

Legal experts have doubts. In Australia, every company must have a director who is responsible if something goes wrong. Professor Jeannie Paterson from the University of Melbourne says the name "zero-human company" is misleading.

The idea comes at a difficult time. Australian tech companies have cut thousands of jobs this year, and many of these cuts have been linked to AI. Junior developer jobs are also disappearing. Photios expects people to react badly, but he hopes AI will help more people start their own businesses.

vocab.en: very close to doing or experiencing something
vocab.example: Scientists say they are on the verge of a breakthrough.

vocab.en: to sell something more cheaply than a competitor
vocab.example: Online stores often undercut local shops on price.

vocab.en: to admit that something is true, often reluctantly
vocab.example: He conceded that the plan had some weaknesses.

vocab.en: to be legally responsible for something
vocab.example: Landlords can be held liable for unsafe buildings.

vocab.en: doubting that something is true or will work
vocab.example: I'm sceptical about diets that promise quick results.

vocab.en: a clever trick used to deceive people
vocab.example: Calling a price rise a 'service upgrade' is just sleight of hand.

vocab.en: to get rid of workers
vocab.example: The airline shed hundreds of jobs during the downturn.

vocab.en: to gradually stop being available
vocab.example: Work dried up for many actors during the strike.

vocab.en: a strong negative reaction from many people
vocab.example: The new parking fees caused a backlash from residents.

questions.q: Ante's product was built in roughly ten days.
questions.explain: 原文说 "Developers created the product in roughly ten days"，故为 True。

questions.q: Photios plans to let AI agents manage Ante's payments.
questions.explain: 原文说他 "is careful... to keep AI away from payments and data security"，与题干相反，故为 False。

questions.q: Ante already has more customers than its main competitor.
questions.explain: 原文提到 Ante 可以 "undercut its rivals"，但没有提到客户数量，故为 Not Given。

questions.q: Why does Jeannie Paterson criticise the term "zero-human company"?
options: Because AI cannot write reliable software
Because such companies pay too little tax
Because a legally compliant firm still needs a responsible human
Because chatbots are banned from selling products
questions.explain: 原文指出每家公司都必须有承担责任的董事，Paterson 认为这种公司其实是 "a sole trader relying heavily on automation"，因此称该说法是 "a terrible sleight of hand"。

stories.discuss: Would you feel comfortable buying from a company run almost entirely by AI? Why or why not, and do you think attitudes will change in the next ten years?

stories.headline: Doctors say they were penalised for having children
stories.headlineZh: 多名医生称因生育而在职业上受到惩罚
stories.summaryZh: 《四角》调查发现，澳大利亚多名医生称因怀孕失去职位或收入，联邦政府仍在考虑改革。
stories.c1:
Several doctors across Australia say they have been penalised for starting a family, according to a Four Corners investigation that found pregnancy discrimination persists across industries, pay levels and locations. In medicine, the accounts suggest that the very structure of training can leave young doctors exposed at the moment they decide to have children.

One trainee in New South Wales, identified only as Alice, says she accepted a three-year training position with the state's health ministry and then told the department she was pregnant. Months before she was due to start, the offer was withdrawn. After she escalated the matter and sought legal advice, she was offered the job again, but only on a two-year contract, and she eventually moved interstate. Another doctor, an emergency registrar, says she kept her pregnancy under wraps until her contract was signed, because she had to reapply for her job every year.

In Tasmania, the head of the state branch of the Australian Medical Association said she had been overwhelmed by the number of doctors who came forward after the investigation. Many reported losing a role for the following year after disclosing a pregnancy, while those forced to move interstate for training risk forfeiting their parental leave entitlements. The Tasmanian health department has acknowledged the problem and says talks are under way.

NSW Health says it cannot comment on individual cases but takes such allegations seriously. At the federal level, the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, Anna Cody, called in October for an overhaul of the law. The government, however, has yet to commit to her recommendations, pointing out that discrimination in employment is already unlawful and saying it is carefully considering the report.
stories.b2:
A number of doctors in Australia say they were treated unfairly because they had children. Their stories come from a Four Corners investigation, which found that pregnancy discrimination still happens in many industries and places. In medicine, the way training works can make young doctors especially vulnerable.

A trainee doctor in New South Wales, called Alice, accepted a three-year training job and then told the health department she was pregnant. Months before she was meant to start, the job offer was taken back. After she complained and got legal advice, she was offered the job again, but only for two years. She later moved to another state. Another doctor hid her pregnancy until her contract was signed, because she had to apply for her job again every year.

In Tasmania, the leader of the local Australian Medical Association branch said many doctors contacted her after the investigation. Some lost a job for the next year after telling their employer they were pregnant. Doctors who move to another state for training can also lose their parental leave.

NSW Health says it takes these complaints seriously. In October, the Sex Discrimination Commissioner, Anna Cody, called for the law to be changed. The federal government says it is still considering her report.

vocab.en: to treat someone unfairly or put them at a disadvantage
vocab.example: The new rules penalise people who work part-time.

vocab.en: to continue to exist, especially when unwanted
vocab.example: If the pain persists, see your doctor.

vocab.zh: 使某人处于易受伤害的境地
vocab.en: to put someone in a vulnerable position
vocab.example: Cutting the safety budget could leave workers exposed.

vocab.en: to take a complaint to a higher level of authority
vocab.example: If the manager ignores you, escalate it to HR.

vocab.en: to keep something secret
vocab.example: They kept their engagement under wraps for months.

vocab.en: to offer information or help, often about something difficult
vocab.example: Police have urged witnesses to come forward.

vocab.en: to lose a right or something because of a rule
vocab.example: If you cancel late, you forfeit your deposit.

vocab.en: already started and happening
vocab.example: Repairs to the bridge are now under way.

vocab.en: a complete change to improve a system
vocab.example: The tax system is badly in need of an overhaul.

questions.q: Alice's training offer was originally for three years.
questions.explain: 原文说她接受了 "a three-year training position"，故为 True。

questions.q: Alice took legal action and won compensation from the health ministry.
questions.explain: 原文只说她 "sought legal advice" 后重新获得职位，并未提及赔偿，故为 Not Given。

questions.q: The federal government has agreed to adopt all of Anna Cody's recommendations.
questions.explain: 原文说政府 "has yet to commit to her recommendations"，故为 False。

questions.q: Why did the emergency registrar hide her pregnancy?
options: Her hospital had a rule against pregnant staff
She had to reapply for her job every year
She was planning to move interstate
She wanted to avoid losing a pay rise
questions.explain: 原文说她隐瞒怀孕 "because she had to reapply for her job every year"。

stories.discuss: Why do you think pregnancy discrimination still happens even though it is illegal? What changes would make workplaces fairer for parents?

dialogue.title: Planning a Busy Saturday
dialogue.setting: Two housemates in Coburg plan their Saturday, which falls on Victorian state election day.
dialogue.settingZh: 两位住在科堡的室友商量周六的安排——那天恰好是维州州选举日。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: So what's the plan for Saturday? Are you still keen on doing something?
lines.zh: 那周六打算干嘛？你还想出去玩吗？

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Definitely, but I need to vote first. It's election day, remember?
lines.zh: 当然想，不过我得先去投票。那天是选举日，记得吧？

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Oh, of course. I'm planning to vote early in the morning and get it out of the way.
lines.zh: 哦对。我打算一大早去投票，先把这事搞定。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Smart move. The queues at our local primary school were massive last time.
lines.zh: 聪明。上次我们附近那所小学排队排得超长。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: And we can't skip the democracy sausage afterwards. That's non-negotiable.
lines.zh: 投完票可不能错过“民主香肠”，这个没得商量。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Ha, fair enough. After that, fancy checking out the Barbie exhibition at Melbourne Museum?
lines.zh: 哈，有道理。之后要不要去墨尔本博物馆看芭比展？

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Seriously? I didn't have you pegged as a Barbie fan.
lines.zh: 真的假的？我可没想到你是芭比粉。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: I'm not, really, but apparently it's more about design and branding than dolls.
lines.zh: 其实也不算，但听说展览更多讲的是设计和品牌，而不只是娃娃。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Fair point. My mum never let me have one, so I'm kind of curious.
lines.zh: 说得也是。我妈小时候从来不让我玩芭比，所以我还挺好奇的。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Apparently they've got the very first Barbie from 1959. That'd be worth seeing.
lines.zh: 据说他们有1959年的第一代芭比，挺值得一看的。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Count me in. Should we book tickets, or just rock up on the day?
lines.zh: 算我一个。我们要提前订票，还是当天直接去？

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Opening day might be packed, so I'd book ahead just to be on the safe side.
lines.zh: 开展第一天可能人很多，保险起见我觉得还是提前订吧。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Good call. I'll sort the tickets if you shout lunch.
lines.zh: 好主意。你请吃午饭的话，票我来搞定。

lines.name: Declan
lines.en: Deal. As long as lunch isn't another sausage from the polling booth!
lines.zh: 成交。只要午饭不是投票站的又一根香肠就行！
